title: First Day for M Bouquets
statement:
A flower bed is a single row. Flower i opens on day bloomDay[i] and stays open after that.

A bouquet needs k open flowers that stand next to each other in the row, and each flower can go into only one bouquet. Return the earliest day on which you can make m bouquets, or -1 if there are not enough flowers ever.

examples.why: By day 6 four flowers are open (positions 0, 2, 4, 5), enough in number, but only 4 and 5 are neighbours. You must wait until day 9.
Two bouquets of two need four flowers, and the bed has three.
On day 2 the pairs at positions 2–3 and 5–6 are open. The flower at 0 is open too, but alone.

hints: If you can make m bouquets by day d, can you also make them by day d + 1? What does that say about the set of good days?
The answer is monotone, so binary search on the day itself, between the smallest and largest bloom day.
To test a day d, walk the row counting consecutive open flowers; every time the run reaches k, count a bouquet and reset the run to 0.

explain.intuition:
Directly picking which flowers form which bouquets is messy. Flip the question: given a day d, can we make m bouquets? That check is a simple greedy walk: count open flowers in a row, cut a bouquet as soon as the run hits k, and reset the run whenever you meet a closed flower. Cutting as early as possible never hurts, because the flowers left over in a run can only be used later in the same run.

Waiting longer never closes a flower, so if day d works, every later day works too. A yes/no answer that flips once is exactly what binary search needs: search for the first day where the check says yes. That takes about 30 checks of O(n) each.
steps: If m × k > n, return -1: there are not enough flowers.
Set lo to the smallest bloom day and hi to the largest; hi always works.
While lo < hi: let mid = ⌊(lo + hi) / 2⌋. If canMake(mid), set hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1.
canMake(d): walk the row, run++ for each flower with bloomDay ≤ d, reset on a closed one; when run === k, count a bouquet and reset.
pitfalls: Counting open flowers in total and dividing by k. Flowers must be adjacent: in [1, 1, 1, 9, 1] four flowers are open on day 1 but only one pair is adjacent.
Computing m × k in 32-bit integers in other languages: 10⁶ × 10⁵ overflows.
Forgetting to reset the run after a bouquet is cut, so one flower is counted in two bouquets.

complexity.time: O(n log D), D = largest bloom day

solutions.title: Try every candidate day
solutions.idea: The answer is one of the bloom days. Check them in increasing order and return the first that works.

solutions.title: Binary search on the day
solutions.idea: Being able to finish by day d is monotone in d. Binary search the first good day with a greedy O(n) check.

followups: Binary search over the sorted distinct bloom days instead of the whole range. Does it change the complexity?
The bed is circular, so the first and last flowers are neighbours. What changes in the check?
